fetched_contents.text: Disease modifying treatment guidelines for multiple sclerosis in the United Arab Emirates Highlights • First ever UAE guideline for MS- an amalgamation of international best practice. • Pragmatic and algorithmic approach after stratifying MS and DMT. • DMT of same class or biosimilars are considered similarly effective. e.g. ocrelizumab and rituximab. • Treatments for RIS and PIRA; AHSCT as second line for aggressive MS. • Recommendations for DMT use in paediatric onset MS pregnancy and breastfeeding. Abstract The newly constituted National Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Society (NMSS)of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), set up a scientific committee to create a MS disease modifying treatment (DMT) guideline for UAE. The committee considered several unique features of the MS community in UAE including large number of expatriate population, wide variations in health insurance coverage, physician and patient preferences for DMT. The overall goal of the treatment guideline is to facilitate the most appropriate DMT to the widest number of patients. To this end it has adapted recommendations from various health systems and regulatory authorities into a pragmatic amalgamation of best practices from across the world. Importantly where data is unavailable or controversial, a common sense approach is taken rather than leave physicians and patients in limbo. The committee classifies MS into subcategories and suggests appropriate treatment choices. It recommends treatment of RIS and CIS with poor prognostic factors. It largely equates the efficacy and safety of DMT with similar mechanisms of action or drug classes e.g. ocrelizumab is similar to rituximab. It allows early switching of treatment for unambiguous disease activity and those with progression independent of relapses. Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be offered to patients who fail one high efficacy DMT. Pragmatic guidance on switching and stopping DMT, DMT choices in pregnancy, lactation and pediatric MS have been included. It is expected that these guidelines will be updated periodically as new data becomes available. Keywords 1. Multiple Sclerosis 2. Disease modifying treatment 3. National guideline 4. United Arab Emirates 5. Middle East 6. Gulf 7. UAE 1 Introduction The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is home to about 10 million people, of which one million are Emirati citizens. UAE is considered a country with medium prevalence for Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Estimates of prevalence are crude and range from 57/100,000 increasing to 64/100,000 when age-standardised (Inshasi & Thakre, 2011, Schiess et al., 2016, Mohammed, 2016). MS is more common in native Emirati people than in a mixed population of Emiratis and expatriates with the majority having relapsing MS (Schiess et al., 2016). All neurologists (not necessarily MS specialists) can manage MS. Primary care systems are not well established in UAE and patients self-refer to hospitals. Onward referrals to larger centres with expertise is uncommon, unless patients themselves chose to do so. Most MS Disease modifying treatments (DMT) are available in UAE. While UAE has a medical regulatory authority, its role has not yet extended into appraisals of individual medicines or cost effectiveness. Therefore, adoption of recommendations by the Food and Drug Administration(FDA) or European Medicines Agency (EMA) is the standard practice. There is presently no guideline for MS DMT in UAE. So, Neurologists use FDA, EMA approved drugs that are available in UAE as per their preferences and guided by the American Academy of Neurology (AAN), European Academy of Neurology (EAN) and Middle East North Africa Committee for Treatment and Research in MS (MENACTRIMS) guidelines (Yamout et al., 2024). This pragmatic approach combined with affordability (UAE per capita GDP is 44,315 USD compared to the EU 38,411 USD) (GDP comparision UAE and EU) has helped the quick introduction of new drugs in UAE once approved in North America or Europe. However, there are disadvantages to the use of “only approved treatments” approach. The health insurance coverage for many expatriates is limited and often excludes licenced MS DMTs due to high cost. Rituximab, a highly effective anti CD20 agent that is far cheaper and used widely in Scandinavian and other Arab countries is denied by insurers as it does not have a formal licence in MS. Early adoption of emerging treatments is limited. For example, autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (AHSCT) used in Europe and USA for aggressive MS has just become available in UAE. The newly constituted National MS Society (NMSS) of UAE, cognizant of the wide variations in health insurance coverage for the UAE resident population and the wide variations in patient and physician preferences, set up a task force to create a UAE MS guideline considering the several unique features of the MS ecosystem in UAE. The overall goal of the treatment guideline is to facilitate the most appropriate DMT to the widest number of patients. To this end it has adapted recommendations from various health systems and regulatory authorities into a pragmatic amalgamation of best practices from across the world (Yamout et al., 2024, Cross & Riley, 2022, Wiendl et al., 2021, Montalban et al., 2018,9, Chitnis et al., 2018, Rae-Grant et al., 2018, Claflin et al., 2019, Simonsen et al., 2021, National MS Society USA 2023, NHS England 2019, Yamout et al., 2020). Importantly where data is unavailable or controversial, a common sense approach is taken rather than leave physicians and patients in limbo. This guideline is not intended to be an exhaustive review of MS or the individual drugs and their data on safety or efficacy. It also does not cover symptomatic treatments, rehabilitation or disorders other than multiple sclerosis. The content of the document is dynamic and may be revised as new information becomes available. The purpose of this document is to assist practitioners in clinical decision-making, to standardize and improve the quality of patient care, and to promote cost-effective drug prescribing. THE CLINICIAN SHOULD USE THESE CLINICAL RECOMMENDATIONSAND INTERPRET IT IN THE CLINICAL CONTEXT OF THE INDIVIDUAL PATIENT. This document should also be used within the context of each DMT's respective Prescribing Information Abbreviations: AAN: American Academy of Neurology; ADR: adverse drug reaction; AE: adverse event; ARR: annualized relapse rate; BID: twice daily; BP: blood pressure; CBC (w/diff): complete blood count (with differential); CDP: confirmed disability progression (CDP-3: at three months; CDP-6: at six months); CFU: Criteria for Use; CIS: clinically isolated syndrome; CMP: complete metabolic panel; CV: cardiovascular; DMT: disease modifying therapy; EDSS: expanded disability status scale; EKG: electrocardiogram; FDA: Food and Drug Administration; Gd: gadolinium; GI: gastrointestinal; HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus; IM: intramuscular; IV: intravenous; IVP: intravenous push; JCV: John Cunningham Virus; LFT: liver function tests; MRI: magnetic resonance imaging; MS: multiple sclerosis; OSA: obstructive sleep apnea; PA-F: facility-level prior authorization; PI: prescribing information; PML: progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy; PO: by mouth; PPMS: primary progressive multiple sclerosis; REMS: Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy; RRMS: relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; S1PR: sphingosine 1-phosphate receptor; SJS: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome; SPMS: secondary progressive multiple sclerosis; SubQ: subcutaneous; TB: Tuberculosis; TEN: toxic epidermal necrolysis; TSH: thyroid stimulating hormone; UA: urinalysis; VZV: Varicella Zoster Virus Introduction This document is intended to provide clinical recommendations to providers in selecting an initial DMT for relapsing forms of MS (includes RRMS and active SPMS) and PPMS. Also, it is to provide considerations regarding when to switch, escalate, de-escalate, and discontinue DMT based on the current level of evidence and expert opinion. The selection of DMT should consider the Veteran's initial and current levels of MS disease activity category, age, and other comorbid conditions. Use of DMT for MS Basic principles of DMTs: * DMTs reduce but do not eliminate rate of relapses and disability accumulation. * DMTs have not been shown to treat progression independent of relapse activity in people with RRMS and SPMS. * DMTs do not treat chronic MS symptoms. The goal is to prevent relapses. * Consider patient-specific factors when choosing a DMT: beliefs about disease and treatment approach, DMT route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. * DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms. Approaches to symptom management may include pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions (e.g., healthy diet, regular exercise/physical therapy, sleep optimization, and management of co-morbid diseases). * Most DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk. This means low efficacy DMTs tend to have a low level of risk, whereas high efficacy DMTs have a high level of risk associated with them. See DMTs in MS Clinical Recommendations Figure 1. Thus, making decisions about starting and switching DMTs include the need to balance patient- specific risks and benefits. * De-escalation and discontinuing DMT is a shift of focus from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management. * MS relapses tend to become less frequent with age. De-escalation and/or discontinuation of DMT may reduce risk of side effects for older patients. * There is no consensus regarding timing for DMT discontinuation, but older patients with prolonged stability on lower efficacy therapies are more likely to discontinue DMT without subsequent disease activity. * Providers should remain vigilant in monitoring for disease activity following DMT discontinuation or de- escalation. "Highly" and "minimally" active disease are commonly used terms to define severity of relapsing MS. That said, disease activity is widely variable and exists on a spectrum of more and less active. Providers will need to take into account many aspects (clinical symptoms, imaging, relapse history, etc.) to determine if a patient with relapsing MS is closer to "highly" or "minimally" active. Criteria below are drawn from clinical practice guidelines, clinical trial entry criteria, natural history studies, and expert opinion. Published in final edited form as: J Immunol Clin Res. 2016 Dec 7;5(1):1032. Abstract Relapses are the hallmark features of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS). True relapses may be challenging to accurately diagnose. A clinician must rely on a combination of history, exam findings, laboratory studies, and neuroimaging to decide whether or not to treat for a presumed relapse. Although many consider MRI as the gold standard diagnostic test, it may not be rapidly accessible and still could miss lesions. In light of this diagnostic complexity, future directions including development and validation of a scale to assess MS relapse probability and severity would be useful to multiple sclerosis specialists and practicing neurologists. Given the complex pathophysiology of MS, more research is needed to ascertain the validity of promising biomarkers for predicting relapse. INTRODUCTION Relapses are the defining features of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS). Approximately 85% to 90% of patients with MS will experience one or more relapses, also called flares or exacerbations, at some point in the course of their disease [1]. The standard definition of an MS relapse as stated in the revised McDonald Criteria is a “patient-reported or objectively observed event typical of an acute inflammatory demyelinating event in the central nervous system, current or historical, with the duration of at least 24 hours in the absence of fever or infection” [2]. Common symptoms of an MS relapse MS relapses can manifest as a wide array of symptoms. Among the most frequent are sensory symptoms, such as numbness and tingling (54.3%), and visual symptoms (21.5%) [3]. Other features include imbalance from cerebellar involvement, extremity weakness, and bladder and bowel dysfunction from spinal cord involvement of the pyramidal tracts. MS relapses associated with pyramidal signs, cerebellar involvement, or sphincter dysfunction tend to be more severe and require prompt identification and treatment. In contrast, patients with sensory, visual, and brainstem symptoms may have a more complete recovery and not necessarily require immediate treatment. Cerebellar relapses are more common in patients who are male, older, and have progressive disease, whereas women tend to exhibit more sensory or visual symptoms [4]. In general, relapse severity increases and recovery decreases with age and with more advanced disease [4]. MS relapse assessment options The physical exam is the most important tool for assessing MS relapse. This involves assessing vital signs, which may reveal alterations in temperature, blood pressure, and heart rate. A thorough neurological exam should include assessment of vision, strength, sensation, gait, and coordination. Vision testing consists of examining visual acuity, color vision, eye movements, and visual fields. Abnormal or new findings on vision testing may indicate a new episode of optic neuritis. In addition, optical coherence tomography (OCT) and visual evoked potentials (VEPs) are adjunctive studies that are increasingly being utilized to provide objective evidence of a patient’s complaint. The neurological exam may also uncover brainstem findings including double vision, altered facial sensation, and speech changes. Abnormalities in a patient’s strength and sensory exams could point to transverse myelitis. Difficulties with gait, coordination, and tremor are often referable to the cerebellum. The neurological examination should always be compared to previously documented exams since new findings may indicate a new relapse or progression of symptoms. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has also been an essential tool in diagnosing and monitoring MS disease activity and progression over time. When a patient’s subjective complaint, such as numbness, can be correlated with new objective findings on an MRI study, this argues for a true relapse. There are unique utilities with different sequences of MRI. For example, T2 FLAIR sequences generally measure the total disease burden based on the accumulated number and size of brain lesions. Meanwhile, gadolinium-enhancing T1 lesions are indicative of breakdown of the blood-brain barrier and signal recent disease activity. Therefore, finding a new lesion, especially a gadolinium-enhancing lesion that corresponds to a patient’s new symptoms, lends support to the diagnosis of a true relapse. However, determining a relapse should not exclusively rely on MRI findings, as new lesions may not be apparent immediately on imaging. Also, the imaging study may not encompass the pertinent area of the nervous system affected (e.g., lesion evidence on MRI orbit but not MRI brain). Sometimes it is necessary to scan the entire spinal axis if transverse myelitis is suspected. However, since this can be time-intensive and cost-prohibitive, a practitioner needs to carefully choose the most appropriate imaging location and modality based on localizing information gathered during the history and examination. A key consideration is the need to rule out fever, metabolic disturbances, infection, or other altered physiological processes to differentiate a true relapse from a “pseudo-relapse.” True relapses are associated with new or worsening symptoms that persist at least 1–3 days, and the recovery phase may span weeks or even months. In contrast, pseudo-relapses are acutely worsening symptoms that are typically associated with an increase in body temperature due to infection, heat exposure, or exercise. fetched_contents.text: Safety of disease-modifying therapies in multiple sclerosis: real-world data from the Austrian MS Treatment Registry (AMSTR) Abstract Background In the therapeutic landscape of multiple sclerosis (MS), more than a dozen disease-modifying therapies (DMT) are currently available. In Austria, only certified MS centers are authorized to prescribe DMT and are obliged to enter patient data into the Austrian MS Therapy Registry (AMSTR). Here, we report the safety profiles of different DMT documented in this registry. Methods Adverse events (AE) data from the AMSTR, collected at least biannually from August 2006 to July 2025, were extracted. AE were classified by system organ classes according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities. Results This analysis included 7913 patients (67.7% female, median age 37 years [IQ 29–45]), with the majority receiving dimethyl fumarate (2572/7913, 32.5%), followed by fingolimod (2129/7913, 26.9%) and natalizumab (2021/7913, 25.5%). For alemtuzumab, the most frequent AE were immune-related (41/90, 45.5%) including thyroid disorders (24/90, 26.7%). For cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab and ofatumumab, infections constituted the most common AE (21/458, 4.6%; 123/2021, 6.1%; 27/698, 3.9%; 16/792, 2%). Gastrointestinal AE were most frequently observed with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide (364/2572, 14.2%, and 78/781, 10%, respectively), whereas AE related to the blood system were most common with sphingosine-1 phosphate receptor modulators (S1P-modulators; fingolimod: 245/2129, 11.5%). Regarding neoplasms, all DMT showed low rates, though S1P-modulators had the highest (fingolimod 31/2129, 1.4%—13/31 [42%] basal cell carcinomas). Conclusions The safety data from the AMSTR do not reveal any new safety issues, particularly regarding neoplasms and infections. Hence, people with MS as well as their treating neurologists are reassured to continue treatment with DMT, as the benefit-risk profile of DMT could be reaffirmed. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00415-025-13473-7. Keywords: Multiple sclerosis, Disease-modifying therapy, Adverse events, Registry Introduction Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory disease of the central nervous system and affects over 2.8 million people worldwide with about 13,500 people in Austria [1]. While the therapeutic landscape of both relapse therapy and symptomatic therapy has not undergone major changes in the last decades, a wide range of disease-modifying therapies (DMT) has emerged over the last 30 years [2]. In general, DMT achieve their disease-modifying effect via immunomodulation and/or immunosuppression [3]. However, especially in the era of highly effective therapies and the related recommendation to the “hit hard and early” concept, the consideration of potential adverse events (AE) and risks is becoming increasingly important [4]. In addition to drug-specific AE, immunomodulation/suppression is especially suspected to increase the risk of infection and cancer [5, 6]. With the ongoing development of new and increasingly effective DMT, the challenges are not only growing for MS research and treatment centers, but they are also impacting healthcare systems on the whole [7]. Consequently, the Central European MS Expert Panel recommended the continuous use and evaluation of registries [8]. The Austrian Multiple Sclerosis Therapy Registry (AMSTR) was therefore set up in 2006, with over 100 MS centers accessing the registry and therefore covering the vast majority of people with MS (pwMS) in Austria [9]. Within the registry, data from approximately 8000 MS patients are being collected continuously and it therefore provides important information on safety, efficacy and treatment adherence in a real-world setting. The aim of this study is to retrospectively analyze safety data on several DMT from the AMSTR in order to search for potential new safety signals in the therapy of MS on a real-world, nation-wide basis in Austria. Methods In Austria, there is a comprehensive network of certified MS centres, hospital based as well as office-based ones. This network provides high-quality patient care and support throughout Austria and ensures appropriate application and monitoring of DMT treatments. The AMSTR was launched in 2006 to collect data on the efficacy and safety of approved DMT in a real-world setting and thereby monitor potential emerging long-term effects and risks [10]. In order to achieve the most comprehensive coverage of patients possible, data entry into the AMSTR is mandatory to fulfil the reimbursement requirements of the Austrian health insurance funds. Of note, the AMSTR is a secure web-based platform that requires online documentation during patient visits by treating neurologists in all Austrian MS centres. In order to improve the quality and reliability of the documented data, an independent data monitoring board was established [11]. The initial entry of baseline data into the AMSTR includes, besides others, MS onset and disease duration, relapses in the prior 12 months, expanded disability status scale (EDSS), and previous DMT use. The follow-up data include in particular EDSS, relapse rate and AE as well as change or discontinuation of treatment and is required to be captured every 3–6 months. In the case of treatment withdrawal, data regarding the reason for discontinuation are queried. In this study, data were obtained from the AMSTR in the period from August 2006 to July 2025. AE`s in temporal and causal relation to drug therapy were classified by system organ classes according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA). Mini-report on which DMTs are most relevant for a patient with new MS symptoms

The evidence points to a clear distinction between relapsing activity and progressive disease in guiding DMT selection. The VA guidance says DMTs reduce but do not eliminate relapse and disability accumulation, and that DMTs do not treat progression independent of relapse activity in relapsing-remitting MS and active secondary progressive MS [N1-F2]. It also emphasizes that treatment choice should consider disease activity category, age, and comorbid conditions, and that decisions should balance patient-specific risks and benefits [N1-F2]. This is important because new symptoms may be interpreted either as relapse activity or as progression, depending on the clinical context [N3-F3].

For new relapse activity, the evidence supports starting or switching DMTs when there is evidence of active disease. The VA guidance states that providers should determine the patient’s MS activity category at first presentation and again periodically for switching, escalating, de-escalating, or discontinuing DMT [N1-F2]. It defines highly active disease broadly, including multiple clinical or radiographic relapses per year while on lower- to moderate-efficacy relapsing MS DMT, or presenting within 5 years of disease onset with high-risk features such as myelopathic relapses, infratentorial signs, incomplete recovery, or high burden T2 lesions [N1-F2]. This means that for a patient with new neurological symptoms suggestive of relapse, the most relevant DMT classes are those used for relapsing MS, especially when the patient is in a highly active category.

The UAE guidelines similarly recommend treatment of RIS (relapse, incomplete recovery, or persistent symptoms) and CIS with poor prognostic factors [N1-F1]. They also note that DMTs of the same class or biosimilars are considered similarly effective and that early switching is allowed for unambiguous disease activity and progression independent of relapses [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that, for a patient with new symptoms that are clearly active, switching DMTs within a class or moving to a more effective class may be appropriate.

For progressive symptoms, the evidence is more cautious. The VA guidance explicitly states that DMTs do not treat progression independent of relapse activity in RRMS and SPMS [N1-F2]. This implies that for a patient with new non-relapse-related symptoms that suggest disease progression, the priority is not necessarily a new DMT aimed at relapse suppression alone, but rather a reassessment of whether progression is occurring and whether treatment strategy should shift from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines also mention autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as a second-line option for aggressive MS after one high-efficacy DMT, which suggests that progressive disease may be handled by escalation or more aggressive therapy rather than simply a standard relapsing DMT [N1-F1].

Treatment choice also depends on disease course and previous response. The VA guidance says the selection should consider the patient’s initial and current MS disease activity category, age, comorbid conditions, and the patient’s route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. It also notes that most DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk, so low-efficacy DMTs tend to have low risk and high-efficacy DMTs high risk [N1-F2]. This means that for a patient with a history of good response but now experiencing new symptoms, the choice may depend on whether the patient remains in a lower-efficacy category or has moved to a more active category, and whether the benefits of switching outweigh the risks. The UAE guidelines further state that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity, and that autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be offered after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F1]. So the prior response history is important: if a patient has failed a previous DMT, the next step may be a different class or a more aggressive therapy, not just a continuation of the same DMT [N1-F1].

For patients with new neurological symptoms, the most relevant DMT classes are those used for relapsing MS. The VA guidance specifically says the document is intended to provide clinical recommendations for selecting an initial DMT for relapsing forms of MS, including RRMS and active SPMS, and also for PPMS [N1-F2]. It also notes that the goal of DMT is to prevent relapses and that DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms [N1-F2]. So for a patient with new neurological symptoms, the most relevant DMTs are those used in relapsing MS, with the choice depending on disease activity category and patient-specific factors [N1-F2].

For patients with new non-neurological symptoms, the evidence is more indirect. The VA guidance says that symptom management may include pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions, and that DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines do not explicitly list non-neurological symptom classes, but they do emphasize that early switching is allowed for unambiguous disease activity and that treatment choices should be made in the context of patient preferences and insurance coverage [N1-F1]. The broader point is that non-neurological symptoms such as fatigue, bladder dysfunction, spasticity, or other symptoms should not be treated as if they are relapse signals alone; rather, they should be managed symptomatically while the DMT strategy is reassessed [N1-F2].

Overall, the most relevant DMT classes for a patient with new MS symptoms are the relapsing-MS DMTs used in RRMS and active SPMS, with the choice depending on disease activity, prior response, and patient-specific factors [N1-F2][N1-F1]. If new symptoms suggest relapse, switching within a class or to a more effective class may be appropriate. If symptoms suggest progression, the focus may shift toward reassessing progression and considering more aggressive therapy rather than simply adding another relapsing DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1].

Mini-report on symptom management and when treatment may change

The evidence shows that symptom-specific treatments can significantly improve quality of life. The symptom management article states that good quality sleep is important in managing fatigue and cognitive symptoms, and that sleep can be disturbed by pain, bladder dysfunction, and spasticity [N2-R1]. It also notes that fatigue, gait impairment, spasticity, tremor, sphincter dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, and other manifestations become increasingly common with disease progression [N2-R2]. The Cleveland Clinic article on bladder dysfunction recommends intermittent catheterization as a preferred treatment for impaired emptying caused by detrusor hypoactivity or other issues [N2-R3]. The Continuum article says tolterodine tartrate has been used for bladder spasticity and that symptomatic treatment may be used for symptoms from MS, fatigue, or depression [N2-R4]. The National MS Society lists FDA-approved medications and devices for treating MS symptoms, including Ampyra for walking difficulties and Baclofen for spasticity [N2-R5]. These examples illustrate that symptom-specific treatments are an important part of care and can help with fatigue, spasticity, bladder dysfunction, and other common MS symptoms [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].

The evidence also helps distinguish when new symptoms suggest relapse rather than just disease progression. The VA guidance says that relapse is defined as a new or recurrent neurological symptom present constantly for 24–48 hours without improvement, and that true relapses may be challenging to diagnose [N3-F3]. It emphasizes that providers should rely on history, exam findings, laboratory studies, and neuroimaging to decide whether to treat for a presumed relapse [N3-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic article notes that a typical MS relapse evolves over 24–48 hours and reaches a nadir in several days, and that more sudden or gradual symptoms should prompt evaluation of alternative causes [N3-R5]. The relapse assessment article explains that the neurological examination should be compared to previously documented exams, because new findings may indicate a new relapse or progression of symptoms [N3-F3]. The relapse definition article also states that a relapse is a patient-reported or objectively observed event typical of an acute inflammatory demyelinating event in the CNS, lasting at least 24 hours in the absence of fever or infection [N3-R2]. These points together show that new neurological symptoms should be interpreted carefully: if they are acute, persistent, and meet relapse criteria, they are more likely to represent relapse; if they are new but not clearly relapse-like, they may reflect progression or other causes [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5].

The evidence also shows how symptom burden can influence treatment re-evaluation. The VA guidance states that DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms and that symptom management may include pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions [N1-F2]. It also says that de-escalation and discontinuation of DMT should be considered when the patient is older, relapses become less frequent, and the goal shifts from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines similarly mention pragmatic guidance on switching and stopping DMT, and that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity [N1-F1]. The VA guidance also emphasizes that the selection of DMT should consider patient-specific factors such as beliefs about disease and treatment approach, DMT route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. This means that when a patient has a high symptom burden, especially if symptoms affect quality of life and daily function, the treatment strategy may need to shift from strict relapse control to a more balanced approach that includes symptom management and possibly de-escalation or discontinuation of DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence does not provide a single numeric threshold for symptom burden, but it does support re-evaluation when symptoms become burdensome or when the patient’s experience of disease activity changes [N1-F2][N3-F3].

In summary, the evidence supports symptom-specific treatments for fatigue, sleep, spasticity, bladder dysfunction, and other common MS symptoms [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. New neurological symptoms should be interpreted with care: acute, persistent symptoms meeting relapse criteria are more likely to represent relapse, while other new symptoms may indicate progression or other causes [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. Symptom burden can influence treatment re-evaluation by prompting a shift from relapse control to symptom management and, if appropriate, de-escalation or discontinuation of DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1].
node_outputs.N9:
Mini-report on safety, tolerability, and practical barriers to DMT use

The evidence shows that common side effects affect treatment continuation and can vary by DMT class. The AMSTR abstract reports that gastrointestinal AE were most frequently observed with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, whereas AE related to the blood system were most common with sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators [N4-F4]. It also says that infection-related AE were most common with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab, and that immune-related AE were most common with alemtuzumab [N4-F4]. The VA guidance summarizes that common side effects include headache, mild transaminitis, diarrhea, and transient alopecia, while less common side effects include hypertension and other issues [N4-R2]. The safety overview article notes that interferon-β1’s most common side effects include benign injection site reactions and post-injection flu-like symptoms, with less common lymphopenia and elevation of other markers [N4-R1]. These findings indicate that tolerability differs by DMT class: gastrointestinal effects are prominent with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, blood-related effects with S1P modulators, and infectious or immune-related effects with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, and alemtuzumab [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-F4].

The evidence also highlights infection risks and monitoring requirements for each DMT class. The AMSTR abstract notes that infection-related AE were common with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab [N4-F4]. The VA guidance states that DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk, and that high-efficacy DMTs carry higher risk [N1-F2]. It also emphasizes that providers should remain vigilant in monitoring for disease activity after DMT discontinuation or de-escalation [N1-F2]. The safety monitoring article specifically lists common side effects and mentions that immunomodulation/suppression is suspected to increase infection and cancer risk [N4-R2]. While the cited evidence does not provide a full class-by-class monitoring schedule, it clearly supports that infection risk is an important concern for several DMT classes, and that monitoring is especially important when switching or de-escalating treatment [N4-R2][N4-F4][N1-F2].

Practical barriers to adherence include patient-specific factors, treatment complexity, and side effects. The VA guidance explicitly states that patient-specific factors such as beliefs about disease and treatment approach, DMT route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc., should be considered when choosing a DMT [N1-F2]. It also says that de-escalation and discontinuation may reduce side effect risk for older patients [N1-F2]. The shared decision-making article notes that shared decision-making interventions can have a positive effect on patient adherence to disease-modifying drug therapy in MS care [N5-R1]. The adherence literature further states that factors influencing adherence span patient-related domains such as depression, cognitive difficulties, and treatment satisfaction, as well as treatment-related aspects such as treatment burden and perceived benefit [N5-R3][N5-R5]. The adherence review also reports that patients adherent to DMTs have a reduced risk of relapse, emergency department visits, severe relapses, hospitalizations, and other adverse outcomes [N5-R5]. This means that practical barriers are not only side effects but also the patient’s ability to manage the regimen, beliefs about the treatment, and perceived satisfaction with the therapy [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

The evidence also suggests ways to address adherence barriers. Shared decision-making is one approach that can improve adherence [N5-R1]. Addressing patient-related factors such as depression, cognition, and satisfaction can improve adherence [N5-R3][N5-R5]. For treatment-related barriers, simplifying administration, managing side effects, and using lower-dose options when appropriate can help [N4-F4][N4-R4]. The VA guidance notes that lower dose of dimethyl fumarate may be tried for patients experiencing significant gastrointestinal side effects, although it says whether efficacy is preserved is unclear [N4-R4]. This supports the idea that tolerability can be managed through dose adjustment rather than discontinuation [N4-R4].

Overall, the evidence shows that safety and tolerability vary by DMT class, with gastrointestinal effects common in dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, blood-related effects in S1P modulators, and infection/immune-related effects in cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, and alemtuzumab [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-F4]. # Possible disease-modifying meds for new MS symptoms

If you have new multiple sclerosis (MS) symptoms, the first thing to understand is that **not all new symptoms are the same**. Some may signal a relapse, while others may be part of disease progression or unrelated changes. The evidence also shows that **DMTs are not just for preventing relapses; they are part of a broader treatment plan that balances relapse control, safety, tolerability, and quality of life** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2].

## 1) What kind of DMT is most relevant depending on your symptoms?
The evidence strongly supports a simple rule of thumb: **use relapsing-MS DMTs if your new symptoms look like relapse activity, and consider more aggressive or different strategies if symptoms suggest progression** [N1-F2][N3-F3][N1-F1].

### a) For new relapse activity
If your new symptoms are neurological and look like a relapse, the most relevant DMTs are those used for **relapsing MS**, especially when you are in a highly active disease category [N1-F2][N1-F1]. The VA guidance says that DMTs reduce but do not eliminate relapse and disability accumulation, and that DMT selection should consider your current disease activity category, age, comorbid conditions, and patient-specific factors [N1-F2]. It also notes that most DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk, so high-efficacy DMTs tend to have higher risk [N1-F2].

The UAE guidelines add that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity and that autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F1]. That means, for a patient with clear new relapse-like symptoms, the treatment strategy may shift from continuing the same DMT to switching within a class or moving to a more effective class, depending on your response and risk profile [N1-F1].

### b) For progressive symptoms
If your new symptoms are not clearly relapse-like and instead suggest disease progression, the evidence is more cautious. The VA guidance explicitly states that DMTs do not treat progression independent of relapse activity in relapsing-remitting MS and active secondary progressive MS [N1-F2]. In other words, for progressive disease, the priority is not simply adding another relapsing DMT. Instead, the focus may shift toward reassessing progression and considering more aggressive therapy, such as escalation to a higher-efficacy DMT or even stem cell transplantation after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F2][N1-F1].

### c) For new neurological versus non-neurological symptoms
If your new symptoms are neurological, the most relevant DMTs remain those used for relapsing MS, with the choice depending on disease activity and patient-specific factors [N1-F2][N1-F1]. If your symptoms are non-neurological—such as fatigue, bladder dysfunction, spasticity, or other symptoms—the evidence suggests that these should be managed symptomatically rather than assuming they are relapse signals alone [N1-F2][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].

## 2) How do I know whether my symptoms are a relapse or progression?
The evidence helps you interpret new symptoms carefully. The VA guidance says that a relapse is defined as a new or recurrent neurological symptom present constantly for 24–48 hours without improvement, and that true relapses may be challenging to diagnose [N3-F3]. It also says that providers should rely on history, exam findings, laboratory studies, and neuroimaging to decide whether to treat for a presumed relapse [N3-F3]. The relapse definition article adds that a relapse is a patient-reported or objectively observed event typical of an acute inflammatory demyelinating event in the CNS, lasting at least 24 hours in the absence of fever or infection [N3-R2]. The Cleveland Clinic article notes that a typical MS relapse evolves over 24–48 hours and reaches a nadir in several days, and that more sudden or gradual symptoms should prompt evaluation of alternative causes [N3-R5].

So, the key takeaway is: **if your symptoms are acute, persistent, and meet relapse criteria, they are more likely to represent relapse; if they are new but not clearly relapse-like, they may indicate progression or another cause** [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The neurological examination should also be compared to previously documented exams, because new findings may indicate a new relapse or progression of symptoms [N3-F3].

## 3) When should treatment change or switch?
The evidence shows that treatment change is often guided by **disease activity, tolerability, and patient-specific factors** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N6-R2].

### a) Signs a DMT may no longer be effective or tolerable
The VA guidance says that formal guidelines on switching disease-modifying therapy are not clearly defined, but it emphasizes that treatment decisions should consider patient-specific factors and that DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk [N1-F2]. It also says that de-escalation and discontinuation may be appropriate when the patient is older, relapses become less frequent, and the goal shifts from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines note that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity and that autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be offered after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F1]. The safety monitoring article adds that if an adverse event occurs in the absence of disease activity, the current DMT may be switched to another with a similar efficacy profile [N6-R2].

### b) Real-world switching patterns and practical considerations
In practice, there is no single fixed timeline for switching. The VA guidance states there is no consensus on timing for DMT discontinuation, but older patients with prolonged stability on lower-efficacy therapies are more likely to discontinue DMT without subsequent disease activity [N1-F2]. It also says providers should remain vigilant in monitoring for disease activity after discontinuation or de-escalation [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines support early switching for unambiguous disease activity and pragmatic guidance on switching and stopping DMT [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic article notes that lower-dose dimethyl fumarate may be tried for patients with significant gastrointestinal side effects, though whether efficacy is preserved is unclear [N4-R4]. Taken together, real-world switching depends on disease activity, side effects, age, prior response, and patient preferences rather than a rigid schedule [N1-F2][N1-F1][N4-R4].

### c) How to decide whether to try a different DMT or switch treatment
The evidence suggests a decision-making process that balances objective disease activity with patient preferences and practical factors. The VA guidance says the selection of DMT should consider your initial and current MS activity category, age, comorbid conditions, and patient-specific factors such as beliefs about disease and treatment approach, route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. It also says decisions should balance patient-specific risks and benefits and that de-escalation or discontinuation may be appropriate when the focus shifts from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines similarly state that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity and that autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F1]. The safety monitoring article adds that if an adverse event occurs without disease activity, the current DMT is switched to another with a similar efficacy profile [N6-R2].

So, the practical answer is: **if your symptoms suggest active disease, if your DMT is no longer tolerable, or if your treatment goals change, it is reasonable to consider switching to a different DMT or changing strategy** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N6-R2].

## 4) What are the possible DMTs and how do they differ?
The evidence points to several classes of DMTs, each with different risks and uses:

- **Interferon-β and other interferons**: These are older DMTs, often with injection-related side effects such as benign injection site reactions and post-injection flu-like symptoms [N4-R1].
- **Dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide**: These are oral DMTs, but gastrointestinal side effects are common with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide [N4-F4].
- **Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators**: These include fingolimod, and they are associated with blood-related adverse events [N4-F4].
- **Anti-CD20 agents**: Ocrelizumab is a representative anti-CD20 agent, and the evidence notes that infection-related AE are common with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab [N4-F4].
- **Alemtuzumab**: This class is associated with immune-related AE, including thyroid disorders [N4-F4].

The UAE guidelines also note that DMTs of the same class or biosimilars are considered similarly effective, and that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity [N1-F1].

## 5) What about symptom-specific treatments?
The evidence supports symptom-specific treatments as an important part of care. Good-quality sleep is important in managing fatigue and cognitive symptoms, and sleep can be disturbed by pain, bladder dysfunction, and spasticity [N2-R1]. Fatigue, gait impairment, spasticity, tremor, sphincter dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, and other symptoms become increasingly common with disease progression [N2-R2]. Bladder dysfunction may be managed with intermittent catheterization for impaired emptying [N2-R3]. Tolterodine tartrate has been used for bladder spasticity, and symptomatic treatment may be used for symptoms from MS, fatigue, or depression [N2-R4]. FDA-approved medications and devices for MS symptoms include Ampyra for walking difficulties and Baclofen for spasticity [N2-R5].

So, if you have non-neurological symptoms such as fatigue, bladder dysfunction, or spasticity, the evidence supports treating those symptoms directly with symptom-specific medications and devices [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].

## 6) How do safety, tolerability, and practical barriers affect treatment?
The evidence clearly shows that DMTs differ in side effects and tolerability. The AMSTR abstract reports that gastrointestinal AE were most frequently observed with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, whereas AE related to the blood system were most common with S1P modulators [N4-F4]. Infection-related AE were most common with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab, and immune-related AE were most common with alemtuzumab [N4-F4]. The VA guidance notes that common side effects include headache, mild transaminitis, diarrhea, and transient alopecia, while less common side effects include hypertension and others [N4-R2]. Interferon-β1’s most common side effects include benign injection site reactions and post-injection flu-like symptoms, with less common lymphopenia and elevation of other markers [N4-R1].

Infection risk is especially important for several DMT classes. The safety monitoring article notes that immunomodulation/suppression is suspected to increase infection and cancer risk [N4-R2]. The VA guidance emphasizes that providers should remain vigilant in monitoring for disease activity after DMT discontinuation or de-escalation [N1-F2].

Practical barriers to adherence include patient-specific factors such as beliefs about disease and treatment approach, route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. Shared decision-making interventions can have a positive effect on patient adherence to disease-modifying drug therapy in MS care [N5-R1]. Adherence is also influenced by patient-related factors such as depression, cognition, and treatment satisfaction, as well as treatment-related factors such as treatment burden and perceived benefit [N5-R3][N5-R5]. Patients adherent to DMTs have been shown to have a reduced risk of relapse, emergency department visits, severe relapses, hospitalizations, and other adverse outcomes [N5-R5].

So, if side effects are a problem, practical barriers can be addressed by shared decision-making, dose adjustment, and simplifying treatment [N5-R1][N4-R4].

## 7) Bottom line for patients
If you have **new MS symptoms**, here is what the evidence suggests:

- If your symptoms look like a relapse, use relapsing-MS DMTs and consider switching within a class or moving to a more effective class if your disease is highly active [N1-F2][N1-F1].
- If your symptoms suggest progression, reassess progression and consider more aggressive therapy rather than simply adding another relapsing DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1].
- If your symptoms are non-neurological, manage them symptomatically and do not assume they are relapse signals alone [N1-F2][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].
- If you are experiencing side effects or if your treatment no longer seems right for you, it is reasonable to consider switching DMTs or changing your treatment strategy [N1-F2][N1-F1][N6-R2].
- Safety and tolerability vary by DMT class, so side effects are an important consideration [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-F4].
- Symptom-specific treatments can improve quality of life and should not be ignored [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].
- Adherence depends on patient-specific factors, treatment complexity, and shared decision-making [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

## 8) What should you do next?
The best next step is to **talk to your MS neurologist**. They can help you interpret whether your new symptoms are a relapse, progression, or something else. They can also help you decide whether your current DMT is still the right choice, whether to switch, and whether symptom-specific treatments are needed [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R1].

In short, the evidence supports a personalized approach: **not all new symptoms mean the same thing, and not all DMTs are the same. Your treatment should be tailored to your disease course, symptoms, tolerability, and preferences** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R1].

# Possible disease-modifying meds for new MS symptoms

If you have new multiple sclerosis (MS) symptoms, the first thing to understand is that **not all new symptoms are the same**. Some may signal a relapse, while others may be part of disease progression or unrelated changes. The evidence also shows that **DMTs are not just for preventing relapses; they are part of a broader treatment plan that balances relapse control, safety, tolerability, and quality of life** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2].

## 1) What kind of DMT is most relevant depending on your symptoms?
The evidence strongly supports a simple rule of thumb: **use relapsing-MS DMTs if your new symptoms look like relapse activity, and consider more aggressive or different strategies if symptoms suggest progression** [N1-F2][N3-F3][N1-F1].

### a) For new relapse activity
If your new symptoms are neurological and look like a relapse, the most relevant DMTs are those used for **relapsing MS**, especially when you are in a highly active disease category [N1-F2][N1-F1]. The VA guidance says that DMTs reduce but do not eliminate relapse and disability accumulation, and that DMT selection should consider your current disease activity category, age, comorbid conditions, and patient-specific factors [N1-F2]. It also notes that most DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk, so high-efficacy DMTs tend to have higher risk [N1-F2].

The UAE guidelines add that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity and that autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F1]. That means, for a patient with clear new relapse-like symptoms, the treatment strategy may shift from continuing the same DMT to switching within a class or moving to a more effective class, depending on your response and risk profile [N1-F1].

### b) For progressive symptoms
If your new symptoms are not clearly relapse-like and instead suggest disease progression, the evidence is more cautious. The VA guidance explicitly states that DMTs do not treat progression independent of relapse activity in relapsing-remitting MS and active secondary progressive MS [N1-F2]. In other words, for progressive disease, the priority is not simply adding another relapsing DMT. Instead, the focus may shift toward reassessing progression and considering more aggressive therapy, such as escalation to a higher-efficacy DMT or even stem cell transplantation after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F2][N1-F1].

### c) For new neurological versus non-neurological symptoms
If your new symptoms are neurological, the most relevant DMTs remain those used for relapsing MS, with the choice depending on disease activity and patient-specific factors [N1-F2][N1-F1]. If your symptoms are non-neurological—such as fatigue, bladder dysfunction, spasticity, or other symptoms—the evidence suggests that these should be managed symptomatically rather than assuming they are relapse signals alone [N1-F2][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].

## 2) How do I know whether my symptoms are a relapse or progression?
The evidence helps you interpret new symptoms carefully. The VA guidance says that a relapse is defined as a new or recurrent neurological symptom present constantly for 24–48 hours without improvement, and that true relapses may be challenging to diagnose [N3-F3]. It also says that providers should rely on history, exam findings, laboratory studies, and neuroimaging to decide whether to treat for a presumed relapse [N3-F3]. The relapse definition article adds that a relapse is a patient-reported or objectively observed event typical of an acute inflammatory demyelinating event in the CNS, lasting at least 24 hours in the absence of fever or infection [N3-R2]. The Cleveland Clinic article notes that a typical MS relapse evolves over 24–48 hours and reaches a nadir in several days, and that more sudden or gradual symptoms should prompt evaluation of alternative causes [N3-R5].

So, the key takeaway is: **if your symptoms are acute, persistent, and meet relapse criteria, they are more likely to represent relapse; if they are new but not clearly relapse-like, they may indicate progression or another cause** [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The neurological examination should also be compared to previously documented exams, because new findings may indicate a new relapse or progression of symptoms [N3-F3].

## 3) When should treatment change or switch?
The evidence shows that treatment change is often guided by **disease activity, tolerability, and patient-specific factors** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N6-R2].

### a) Signs a DMT may no longer be effective or tolerable
The VA guidance says that formal guidelines on switching disease-modifying therapy are not clearly defined, but it emphasizes that treatment decisions should consider patient-specific factors and that DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk [N1-F2]. It also says that de-escalation and discontinuation may be appropriate when the patient is older, relapses become less frequent, and the goal shifts from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines note that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity and that autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be offered after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F1]. The safety monitoring article adds that if an adverse event occurs in the absence of disease activity, the current DMT may be switched to another with a similar efficacy profile [N6-R2].

### b) Real-world switching patterns and practical considerations
In practice, there is no single fixed timeline for switching. The VA guidance states there is no consensus on timing for DMT discontinuation, but older patients with prolonged stability on lower-efficacy therapies are more likely to discontinue DMT without subsequent disease activity [N1-F2]. It also says providers should remain vigilant in monitoring for disease activity after discontinuation or de-escalation [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines support early switching for unambiguous disease activity and pragmatic guidance on switching and stopping DMT [N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic article notes that lower-dose dimethyl fumarate may be tried for patients with significant gastrointestinal side effects, though whether efficacy is preserved is unclear [N4-R4]. Taken together, real-world switching depends on disease activity, side effects, age, prior response, and patient preferences rather than a rigid schedule [N1-F2][N1-F1][N4-R4].

### c) How to decide whether to try a different DMT or switch treatment
The evidence suggests a decision-making process that balances objective disease activity with patient preferences and practical factors. The VA guidance says the selection of DMT should consider your initial and current MS activity category, age, comorbid conditions, and patient-specific factors such as beliefs about disease and treatment approach, route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. It also says decisions should balance patient-specific risks and benefits and that de-escalation or discontinuation may be appropriate when the focus shifts from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines similarly state that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity and that autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F1]. The safety monitoring article adds that if an adverse event occurs without disease activity, the current DMT is switched to another with a similar efficacy profile [N6-R2].

So, the practical answer is: **if your symptoms suggest active disease, if your DMT is no longer tolerable, or if your treatment goals change, it is reasonable to consider switching to a different DMT or changing strategy** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N6-R2].

## 4) What are the possible DMTs and how do they differ?
The evidence points to several classes of DMTs, each with different risks and uses:

- **Interferon-β and other interferons**: These are older DMTs, often with injection-related side effects such as benign injection site reactions and post-injection flu-like symptoms [N4-R1].
- **Dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide**: These are oral DMTs, but gastrointestinal side effects are common with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide [N4-F4].
- **Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators**: These include fingolimod, and they are associated with blood-related adverse events [N4-F4].
- **Anti-CD20 agents**: Ocrelizumab is a representative anti-CD20 agent, and the evidence notes that infection-related AE are common with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab [N4-F4].
- **Alemtuzumab**: This class is associated with immune-related AE, including thyroid disorders [N4-F4].

The UAE guidelines also note that DMTs of the same class or biosimilars are considered similarly effective, and that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity [N1-F1].

## 5) What about symptom-specific treatments?
The evidence supports symptom-specific treatments as an important part of care. Good-quality sleep is important in managing fatigue and cognitive symptoms, and sleep can be disturbed by pain, bladder dysfunction, and spasticity [N2-R1]. Fatigue, gait impairment, spasticity, tremor, sphincter dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, and other symptoms become increasingly common with disease progression [N2-R2]. Bladder dysfunction may be managed with intermittent catheterization for impaired emptying [N2-R3]. Tolterodine tartrate has been used for bladder spasticity, and symptomatic treatment may be used for symptoms from MS, fatigue, or depression [N2-R4]. FDA-approved medications and devices for MS symptoms include Ampyra for walking difficulties and Baclofen for spasticity [N2-R5].

So, if you have non-neurological symptoms such as fatigue, bladder dysfunction, or spasticity, the evidence supports treating those symptoms directly with symptom-specific medications and devices [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].

## 6) How do safety, tolerability, and practical barriers affect treatment?
The evidence clearly shows that DMTs differ in side effects and tolerability. The AMSTR abstract reports that gastrointestinal AE were most frequently observed with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, whereas AE related to the blood system were most common with S1P modulators [N4-F4]. Infection-related AE were most common with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab, and immune-related AE were most common with alemtuzumab [N4-F4]. The VA guidance notes that common side effects include headache, mild transaminitis, diarrhea, and transient alopecia, while less common side effects include hypertension and others [N4-R2]. Interferon-β1’s most common side effects include benign injection site reactions and post-injection flu-like symptoms, with less common lymphopenia and elevation of other markers [N4-R1].

Infection risk is especially important for several DMT classes. The safety monitoring article notes that immunomodulation/suppression is suspected to increase infection and cancer risk [N4-R2]. The VA guidance emphasizes that providers should remain vigilant in monitoring for disease activity after DMT discontinuation or de-escalation [N1-F2].

Practical barriers to adherence include patient-specific factors such as beliefs about disease and treatment approach, route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. Shared decision-making interventions can have a positive effect on patient adherence to disease-modifying drug therapy in MS care [N5-R1]. Adherence is also influenced by patient-related factors such as depression, cognition, and treatment satisfaction, as well as treatment-related factors such as treatment burden and perceived benefit [N5-R3][N5-R5]. Patients adherent to DMTs have been shown to have a reduced risk of relapse, emergency department visits, severe relapses, hospitalizations, and other adverse outcomes [N5-R5].

So, if side effects are a problem, practical barriers can be addressed by shared decision-making, dose adjustment, and simplifying treatment [N5-R1][N4-R4].

## 7) Bottom line for patients
If you have **new MS symptoms**, here is what the evidence suggests:

- If your symptoms look like a relapse, use relapsing-MS DMTs and consider switching within a class or moving to a more effective class if your disease is highly active [N1-F2][N1-F1].
- If your symptoms suggest progression, reassess progression and consider more aggressive therapy rather than simply adding another relapsing DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1].
- If your symptoms are non-neurological, manage them symptomatically and do not assume they are relapse signals alone [N1-F2][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].
- If you are experiencing side effects or if your treatment no longer seems right for you, it is reasonable to consider switching DMTs or changing your treatment strategy [N1-F2][N1-F1][N6-R2].
- Safety and tolerability vary by DMT class, so side effects are an important consideration [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-F4].
- Symptom-specific treatments can improve quality of life and should not be ignored [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].
- Adherence depends on patient-specific factors, treatment complexity, and shared decision-making [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

## 8) What should you do next?
The best next step is to **talk to your MS neurologist**. They can help you interpret whether your new symptoms are a relapse, progression, or something else. They can also help you decide whether your current DMT is still the right choice, whether to switch, and whether symptom-specific treatments are needed [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R1].

In short, the evidence supports a personalized approach: **not all new symptoms mean the same thing, and not all DMTs are the same. Your treatment should be tailored to your disease course, symptoms, tolerability, and preferences** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R1].

The evidence points to a clear distinction between relapsing activity and progressive disease in guiding DMT selection. For new relapse activity, the evidence supports starting or switching DMTs when there is evidence of active disease. The VA guidance states that providers should determine the patient’s MS activity category at first presentation and again periodically for switching, escalating, de-escalating, or discontinuing DMT [N1-F2]. It defines highly active disease broadly, including multiple clinical or radiographic relapses per year while on lower- to moderate-efficacy relapsing MS DMT, or presenting within 5 years of disease onset with high-risk features such as myelopathic relapses, infratentorial signs, incomplete recovery, or high burden T2 lesions [N1-F2]. This means that for a patient with new neurological symptoms suggestive of relapse, the most relevant DMT classes are those used for relapsing MS, especially when the patient is in a highly active category.

The UAE guidelines similarly recommend treatment of RIS (relapse, incomplete recovery, or persistent symptoms) and CIS with poor prognostic factors [N1-F1]. They also note that DMTs of the same class or biosimilars are considered similarly effective and that early switching is allowed for unambiguous disease activity and progression independent of relapses [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that, for a patient with new symptoms that are clearly active, switching DMTs within a class or moving to a more effective class may be appropriate.

For progressive symptoms, the evidence is more cautious. The VA guidance explicitly states that DMTs do not treat progression independent of relapse activity in RRMS and SPMS [N1-F2]. This implies that for a patient with new non-relapse-related symptoms that suggest disease progression, the priority is not necessarily a new DMT aimed at relapse suppression alone, but rather a reassessment of whether progression is occurring and whether treatment strategy should shift from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines also mention autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as a second-line option for aggressive MS after one high-efficacy DMT, which suggests that progressive disease may be handled by escalation or more aggressive therapy rather than simply a standard relapsing DMT [N1-F1].

Treatment choice also depends on disease course and previous response. The VA guidance says the selection should consider the patient’s initial and current MS disease activity category, age, comorbid conditions, and the patient’s route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. It also notes that most DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk, so low-efficacy DMTs tend to have low risk and high-efficacy DMTs high risk [N1-F2]. This means that for a patient with a history of good response but now experiencing new symptoms, the choice may depend on whether the patient remains in a lower-efficacy category or has moved to a more active category, and whether the benefits of switching outweigh the risks. For patients with new neurological symptoms, the most relevant DMT classes are those used for relapsing MS. The VA guidance specifically says the document is intended to provide clinical recommendations for selecting an initial DMT for relapsing forms of MS, including RRMS and active SPMS, and also for PPMS [N1-F2]. It also notes that the goal of DMT is to prevent relapses and that DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms [N1-F2]. The VA guidance says that symptom management may include pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions, and that DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms [N1-F2]. Mini-report on which DMTs are most relevant for a patient with new MS symptoms

The evidence points to a clear distinction between relapsing activity and progressive disease in guiding DMT selection. The VA guidance says DMTs reduce but do not eliminate relapse and disability accumulation, and that DMTs do not treat progression independent of relapse activity in relapsing-remitting MS and active secondary progressive MS [N1-F2]. It also emphasizes that treatment choice should consider disease activity category, age, and comorbid conditions, and that decisions should balance patient-specific risks and benefits [N1-F2]. This is important because new symptoms may be interpreted either as relapse activity or as progression, depending on the clinical context [N3-F3].

For new relapse activity, the evidence supports starting or switching DMTs when there is evidence of active disease. The VA guidance states that providers should determine the patient’s MS activity category at first presentation and again periodically for switching, escalating, de-escalating, or discontinuing DMT [N1-F2]. It defines highly active disease broadly, including multiple clinical or radiographic relapses per year while on lower- to moderate-efficacy relapsing MS DMT, or presenting within 5 years of disease onset with high-risk features such as myelopathic relapses, infratentorial signs, incomplete recovery, or high burden T2 lesions [N1-F2]. This means that for a patient with new neurological symptoms suggestive of relapse, the most relevant DMT classes are those used for relapsing MS, especially when the patient is in a highly active category.

The UAE guidelines similarly recommend treatment of RIS (relapse, incomplete recovery, or persistent symptoms) and CIS with poor prognostic factors [N1-F1]. They also note that DMTs of the same class or biosimilars are considered similarly effective and that early switching is allowed for unambiguous disease activity and progression independent of relapses [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that, for a patient with new symptoms that are clearly active, switching DMTs within a class or moving to a more effective class may be appropriate.

For progressive symptoms, the evidence is more cautious. The VA guidance explicitly states that DMTs do not treat progression independent of relapse activity in RRMS and SPMS [N1-F2]. This implies that for a patient with new non-relapse-related symptoms that suggest disease progression, the priority is not necessarily a new DMT aimed at relapse suppression alone, but rather a reassessment of whether progression is occurring and whether treatment strategy should shift from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines also mention autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as a second-line option for aggressive MS after one high-efficacy DMT, which suggests that progressive disease may be handled by escalation or more aggressive therapy rather than simply a standard relapsing DMT [N1-F1].

Treatment choice also depends on disease course and previous response. The VA guidance says the selection should consider the patient’s initial and current MS disease activity category, age, comorbid conditions, and the patient’s route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. It also notes that most DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk, so low-efficacy DMTs tend to have low risk and high-efficacy DMTs high risk [N1-F2]. This means that for a patient with a history of good response but now experiencing new symptoms, the choice may depend on whether the patient remains in a lower-efficacy category or has moved to a more active category, and whether the benefits of switching outweigh the risks. The UAE guidelines further state that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity, and that autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be offered after one high-efficacy DMT fails [N1-F1]. So the prior response history is important: if a patient has failed a previous DMT, the next step may be a different class or a more aggressive therapy, not just a continuation of the same DMT [N1-F1].

For patients with new neurological symptoms, the most relevant DMT classes are those used for relapsing MS. The VA guidance specifically says the document is intended to provide clinical recommendations for selecting an initial DMT for relapsing forms of MS, including RRMS and active SPMS, and also for PPMS [N1-F2]. It also notes that the goal of DMT is to prevent relapses and that DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms [N1-F2]. So for a patient with new neurological symptoms, the most relevant DMTs are those used in relapsing MS, with the choice depending on disease activity category and patient-specific factors [N1-F2].

For patients with new non-neurological symptoms, the evidence is more indirect. The VA guidance says that symptom management may include pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions, and that DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines do not explicitly list non-neurological symptom classes, but they do emphasize that early switching is allowed for unambiguous disease activity and that treatment choices should be made in the context of patient preferences and insurance coverage [N1-F1]. The broader point is that non-neurological symptoms such as fatigue, bladder dysfunction, spasticity, or other symptoms should not be treated as if they are relapse signals alone; rather, they should be managed symptomatically while the DMT strategy is reassessed [N1-F2].

Overall, the most relevant DMT classes for a patient with new MS symptoms are the relapsing-MS DMTs used in RRMS and active SPMS, with the choice depending on disease activity, prior response, and patient-specific factors [N1-F2][N1-F1]. If new symptoms suggest relapse, switching within a class or to a more effective class may be appropriate. If symptoms suggest progression, the focus may shift toward reassessing progression and considering more aggressive therapy rather than simply adding another relapsing DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1].
