Mini-report on symptom management and when treatment may change

The evidence shows that symptom-specific treatments can significantly improve quality of life. The symptom management article states that good quality sleep is important in managing fatigue and cognitive symptoms, and that sleep can be disturbed by pain, bladder dysfunction, and spasticity [N2-R1]. It also notes that fatigue, gait impairment, spasticity, tremor, sphincter dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, and other manifestations become increasingly common with disease progression [N2-R2]. The Cleveland Clinic article on bladder dysfunction recommends intermittent catheterization as a preferred treatment for impaired emptying caused by detrusor hypoactivity or other issues [N2-R3]. The Continuum article says tolterodine tartrate has been used for bladder spasticity and that symptomatic treatment may be used for symptoms from MS, fatigue, or depression [N2-R4]. The National MS Society lists FDA-approved medications and devices for treating MS symptoms, including Ampyra for walking difficulties and Baclofen for spasticity [N2-R5]. These examples illustrate that symptom-specific treatments are an important part of care and can help with fatigue, spasticity, bladder dysfunction, and other common MS symptoms [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].

The evidence also helps distinguish when new symptoms suggest relapse rather than just disease progression. The VA guidance says that relapse is defined as a new or recurrent neurological symptom present constantly for 24–48 hours without improvement, and that true relapses may be challenging to diagnose [N3-F3]. It emphasizes that providers should rely on history, exam findings, laboratory studies, and neuroimaging to decide whether to treat for a presumed relapse [N3-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic article notes that a typical MS relapse evolves over 24–48 hours and reaches a nadir in several days, and that more sudden or gradual symptoms should prompt evaluation of alternative causes [N3-R5]. The relapse assessment article explains that the neurological examination should be compared to previously documented exams, because new findings may indicate a new relapse or progression of symptoms [N3-F3]. The relapse definition article also states that a relapse is a patient-reported or objectively observed event typical of an acute inflammatory demyelinating event in the CNS, lasting at least 24 hours in the absence of fever or infection [N3-R2]. These points together show that new neurological symptoms should be interpreted carefully: if they are acute, persistent, and meet relapse criteria, they are more likely to represent relapse; if they are new but not clearly relapse-like, they may reflect progression or other causes [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5].

The evidence also shows how symptom burden can influence treatment re-evaluation. The VA guidance states that DMT does not eliminate the need to treat MS symptoms and that symptom management may include pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions [N1-F2]. It also says that de-escalation and discontinuation of DMT should be considered when the patient is older, relapses become less frequent, and the goal shifts from relapse control to risk reduction and symptomatic management [N1-F2]. The UAE guidelines similarly mention pragmatic guidance on switching and stopping DMT, and that early switching is acceptable for unambiguous disease activity [N1-F1]. The VA guidance also emphasizes that the selection of DMT should consider patient-specific factors such as beliefs about disease and treatment approach, DMT route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc. [N1-F2]. This means that when a patient has a high symptom burden, especially if symptoms affect quality of life and daily function, the treatment strategy may need to shift from strict relapse control to a more balanced approach that includes symptom management and possibly de-escalation or discontinuation of DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence does not provide a single numeric threshold for symptom burden, but it does support re-evaluation when symptoms become burdensome or when the patient’s experience of disease activity changes [N1-F2][N3-F3].

In summary, the evidence supports symptom-specific treatments for fatigue, sleep, spasticity, bladder dysfunction, and other common MS symptoms [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. New neurological symptoms should be interpreted with care: acute, persistent symptoms meeting relapse criteria are more likely to represent relapse, while other new symptoms may indicate progression or other causes [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. Symptom burden can influence treatment re-evaluation by prompting a shift from relapse control to symptom management and, if appropriate, de-escalation or discontinuation of DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1].

The evidence shows that common side effects affect treatment continuation and can vary by DMT class. The AMSTR abstract reports that gastrointestinal AE were most frequently observed with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, whereas AE related to the blood system were most common with sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators [N4-F4]. It also says that infection-related AE were most common with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab, and that immune-related AE were most common with alemtuzumab [N4-F4]. The VA guidance summarizes that common side effects include headache, mild transaminitis, diarrhea, and transient alopecia, while less common side effects include hypertension and other issues [N4-R2]. The safety overview article notes that interferon-β1’s most common side effects include benign injection site reactions and post-injection flu-like symptoms, with less common lymphopenia and elevation of other markers [N4-R1]. These findings indicate that tolerability differs by DMT class: gastrointestinal effects are prominent with dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, blood-related effects with S1P modulators, and infectious or immune-related effects with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, and alemtuzumab [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-F4].

The evidence also highlights infection risks and monitoring requirements for each DMT class. The AMSTR abstract notes that infection-related AE were common with cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab [N4-F4]. The VA guidance states that DMTs have a positive correlation between efficacy and risk, and that high-efficacy DMTs carry higher risk [N1-F2]. It also emphasizes that providers should remain vigilant in monitoring for disease activity after DMT discontinuation or de-escalation [N1-F2]. The safety monitoring article specifically lists common side effects and mentions that immunomodulation/suppression is suspected to increase infection and cancer risk [N4-R2]. While the cited evidence does not provide a full class-by-class monitoring schedule, it clearly supports that infection risk is an important concern for several DMT classes, and that monitoring is especially important when switching or de-escalating treatment [N4-R2][N4-F4][N1-F2].

Practical barriers to adherence include patient-specific factors, treatment complexity, and side effects. The VA guidance explicitly states that patient-specific factors such as beliefs about disease and treatment approach, DMT route of administration, frequency, side effects, pregnancy planning, self-administration abilities, etc., should be considered when choosing a DMT [N1-F2]. It also says that de-escalation and discontinuation may reduce side effect risk for older patients [N1-F2]. The shared decision-making article notes that shared decision-making interventions can have a positive effect on patient adherence to disease-modifying drug therapy in MS care [N5-R1]. The adherence literature further states that factors influencing adherence span patient-related domains such as depression, cognitive difficulties, and treatment satisfaction, as well as treatment-related aspects such as treatment burden and perceived benefit [N5-R3][N5-R5]. The adherence review also reports that patients adherent to DMTs have a reduced risk of relapse, emergency department visits, severe relapses, hospitalizations, and other adverse outcomes [N5-R5]. This means that practical barriers are not only side effects but also the patient’s ability to manage the regimen, beliefs about the treatment, and perceived satisfaction with the therapy [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

The evidence also suggests ways to address adherence barriers. Shared decision-making is one approach that can improve adherence [N5-R1]. Addressing patient-related factors such as depression, cognition, and satisfaction can improve adherence [N5-R3][N5-R5]. For treatment-related barriers, simplifying administration, managing side effects, and using lower-dose options when appropriate can help [N4-F4][N4-R4]. The VA guidance notes that lower dose of dimethyl fumarate may be tried for patients experiencing significant gastrointestinal side effects, although it says whether efficacy is preserved is unclear [N4-R4]. This supports the idea that tolerability can be managed through dose adjustment rather than discontinuation [N4-R4].

Overall, the evidence shows that safety and tolerability vary by DMT class, with gastrointestinal effects common in dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, blood-related effects in S1P modulators, and infection/immune-related effects in cladribine, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, and alemtuzumab [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-F4]. Infection risk is an important monitoring concern, especially for higher-risk DMTs [N4-R2][N4-F4]. Practical barriers to adherence include patient-specific beliefs, route of administration, frequency, side effects, and adherence-related factors such as depression and treatment satisfaction [N1-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5]. These barriers can be addressed through shared decision-making, dose adjustment, and simplification of treatment regimens [N5-R1][N4-R4].

- If your symptoms look like a relapse, use relapsing-MS DMTs and consider switching within a class or moving to a more effective class if your disease is highly active [N1-F2][N1-F1].
- If your symptoms suggest progression, reassess progression and consider more aggressive therapy rather than simply adding another relapsing DMT [N1-F2][N1-F1].
- If your symptoms are non-neurological, manage them symptomatically and do not assume they are relapse signals alone [N1-F2][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].
- If you are experiencing side effects or if your treatment no longer seems right for you, it is reasonable to consider switching DMTs or changing your treatment strategy [N1-F2][N1-F1][N6-R2].
- Safety and tolerability vary by DMT class, so side effects are an important consideration [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-F4].
- Symptom-specific treatments can improve quality of life and should not be ignored [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].
- Adherence depends on patient-specific factors, treatment complexity, and shared decision-making [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

## 8) What should you do next?
The best next step is to **talk to your MS neurologist**. They can help you interpret whether your new symptoms are a relapse, progression, or something else. They can also help you decide whether your current DMT is still the right choice, whether to switch, and whether symptom-specific treatments are needed [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R1].

In short, the evidence supports a personalized approach: **not all new symptoms mean the same thing, and not all DMTs are the same. Your treatment should be tailored to your disease course, symptoms, tolerability, and preferences** [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R1].
